abstract: BACKGROUND: From November 2018 through February 2019, person-to-person transmission of Andes virus (ANDV) hantavirus pulmonary syndrome occurred in Chubut Province, Argentina, and resulted in 34 confirmed infections and 11 deaths. Understanding the genomic, epidemiologic, and clinical characteristics of person-to-person transmission of ANDV is crucial to designing effective interventions. METHODS: Clinical and epidemiologic information was obtained by means of patient report and from public health centers. Serologic testing, contact-tracing, and next-generation sequencing were used to identify ANDV infection as the cause of this outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome and to reconstruct person-to-person transmission events. RESULTS: After a single introduction of ANDV from a rodent reservoir into the human population, transmission was driven by 3 symptomatic persons who attended crowded social events. After 18 cases were confirmed, public health officials enforced isolation of persons with confirmed cases and self-quarantine of possible contacts; these measures most likely curtailed further spread. The median reproductive number (the number of secondary cases caused by an infected person during the infectious period) was 2.12 before the control measures were enforced and decreased to 0.96 after the measures were implemented. Full genome sequencing of the ANDV strain involved in this outbreak was performed with specimens from 27 patients and showed that the strain that was present (Epuyén/18-19) was similar to the causative strain (Epilink/96) in the first known person-to-person transmission of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome caused by ANDV, which occurred in El Bolsón, Argentina, in 1996. Clinical investigations involving patients with ANDV hantavirus pulmonary syndrome in this outbreak revealed that patients with a high viral load and liver injury were more likely than other patients to spread infection. Disease severity, genomic diversity, age, and time spent in the hospital had no clear association with secondary transmission. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with ANDV hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, high viral titers in combination with attendance at massive social gatherings or extensive contact among persons were associated with a higher likelihood of transmission. (Funded by the Ministerio de Salud y Desarrollo Social de la Nación Argentina and others.).

narrative:
Short impact summary

This 2020 New England Journal of Medicine article has shown clear scholarly uptake, with 226 citations in OpenAlex and a high percentile standing in its field-year context. Its influence is especially visible in later hantavirus, outbreak, and preparedness research, where it is repeatedly cited as a reference point for understanding Andes virus transmission dynamics. The record also shows documented downstream reuse and limited but nontrivial citation-statement evidence, alongside a small amount of contradictory citing discussion.

Full narrative

“Super-Spreaders” and Person-to-Person Transmission of Andes Virus in Argentina became an important reference after documenting a major Andes virus transmission event in Chubut Province, Argentina, with 34 confirmed infections and 11 deaths. The article’s impact is strongest in the scholarly literature: it has accumulated 226 citations, sits in a high field-year percentile, and is repeatedly taken up in work on hantavirus epidemiology, outbreak investigation, and preparedness.

The citing landscape suggests that the paper is not just frequently cited, but cited across a fairly wide research base. Its most visible downstream venues include virology, infectious-disease, travel medicine, and outbreak-oriented journals, with additional attention in preprints and reviews. Recent citing works show that the article continues to serve as a touchstone for contemporary hantavirus discussions, including clinical management, transmission dynamics, neuroinvolvement, wastewater surveillance, and outbreak response.

Evidence from scite indicates that the paper is mainly mentioned rather than deeply argued over: most citation statements are neutral mentions, with a small number of supporting statements and one contradicting statement. That pattern is consistent with a work that is being used as an established source for context and framing, rather than as a site of sustained methodological dispute.

Beyond citations, the record shows broader reuse signals, including downstream reuse in articles, preprints, reviews, book chapters, and other scholarly formats. The article also appears in OpenAIRE repositories and is indexed in PubMed, indicating relatively broad accessibility for a biomedical paper. Public-facing attention is sparse in the available record, but there is some evidence of web-level discussion through specialized outlets such as virology podcasts and epidemiology newsletters, reflecting renewed relevance during later hantavirus developments.

The funding record points to support from U.S. biodefense and infectious-disease research channels as well as Argentine public health institutions, which fits the article’s cross-border, outbreak-response character. Overall, the evidence portrays a paper with durable scholarly influence, especially as a citation anchor for studies of Andes virus transmission, clinical consequences, and preparedness.
